newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka prepares to battle gun culture.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka prepares to battle gun culture.

text.p: Sri Lanka's recent crackdown on illegal firearms is a belated but necessary government reaction to the island's growing culture of violence, politicians and analysts said on Thursday.
"The crackdown has come somewhat later than it should have," columnist and independent analyst Lucien Rajakarunanayake told Reuters.

"But it does show that the government has accepted a reality which many people have been trying to tell them for so long, that there is a ... gun culture in this country," said Rajakarunanayake, president of "Democracy", an independent action group campaigning for freedom of expression.

Sri Lanka, racked by violence ahead of next week's local government elections, plans to enact new laws under emergency regulations against illegal firearms, Justice Minister G.L. Peiris told a news conference on Wednesday.

"Today in Sri Lanka there is a very strong consensus in favour of tougher legislation to deal with illegal firearms," Peiris said. "The existing laws are inadequate and we need tougher ones to control the indiscriminate use of firearms."
Peiris' comments came just three days before a police amnesty to surrender unlicenced weapons expires on Saturday.
So far, police searches and people handing in firearms have netted more than 1,500 illegal weapons, Mohammed Nizam, deputy inspector-general of the police crimes branch, told Reuters.
"We will find out who possesses illegal guns and vigorously pursue them (after the amnesty expires)", Nizam said.
Politicians and party activists in Sri Lanka carry guns, many of them unlicensed, to guard against attack by separatist Tamil rebels who are fighting for independence in the island's north and east.
But often they are used for other purposes, such as intimidating members of opposition political camps, a government parliament deputy said.
"Guns are being used to create a fear psychosis," said Jagath Balasuriya, an MP from the ruling People's Alliance coalition.
"This culture of violence must end. The government has recognised it and made it a priority," he said.
In possibly the most notorious example of Sri Lanka's gun culture, a young member of parliament from the People's Alliance was gunned down last month during a roadside quarrel.
An MP from the main opposition United National Party (UNP) and a former UNP mayor are among the suspects detained by police in connection with the killing.
Police on Friday said they were searching for another UNP legislator in connection with the shooting of an alliance candidate in the election.
But Peiris said the new laws, expected to be finalised within three weeks, were not tied to the local polls.
"It is a pressing social problem and these changes are necessary to guarantee personal safety of the community," he said.
The laws provide for a minimum seven-year prison term and a maximum of 20 years for possession of unlicensed firearms and the confiscation of property where illegal firearms are found.
The government also plans to make bail unavailable to those charged until the judicial process is completed, Peiris said.
"The government's reaction is certainly to send out a message that it is not turning a blind eye to violence," Rajakarunanayake said.
